claim: Previously, using simultaneous resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and photometry-based neuronal calcium recordings in the anesthetized rat, BOLD responses directly related to slow calcium waves were identified, revealing a cortex-wide and spatially organized correlate of locally recorded neuronal activity.
source: Previously, using simultaneous resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and photometry-based neuronal calcium recordings in the anesthetized rat, we identified blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) responses directly related to slow calcium waves, revealing a cortex-wide and spatially organized correlate of locally recorded neuronal activity (Schwalm et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Schwalm et al., 2017) that established this finding.

claim: During persistent activity, compartmentalized network dynamics were observed.
source: persistent activity, in which compartmentalized network dynamics were observed
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing ICA components and connectivity patterns during persistent activity.

claim: During slow wave activity, a cortex-wide BOLD component was observed, suggesting a strong functional coupling of inter-cortical activity.
source: slow wave activity, dominated by a cortex-wide BOLD component, suggesting a strong functional coupling of inter-cortical activity
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing ICA results and connectivity analyses during slow wave activity.

claim: During slow wave activity, there is a correlation between the occurring slow wave events and the strength of functional connectivity between different cortical areas.
source: During slow wave activity, we find a correlation between the occurring slow wave events and the strength of functional connectivity between different cortical areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between down-up transitions and functional connectivity strength.

claim: Down-up transitions of neuronal excitability can drive cortex-wide functional connectivity.
source: These findings suggest that down-up transitions of neuronal excitability can drive cortex-wide functional connectivity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation data between slow wave events and functional connectivity.

claim: Changes in functional connectivity are dependent on the brain's current state, directly linked to the generation of slow waves.
source: This study provides further evidence that changes in functional connectivity are dependent on the brain's current state, directly linked to the generation of slow waves.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data comparing connectivity patterns across different brain states.

claim: Default-mode networks have been identified in humans.
source: The resting-state of the cortical functional architecture is characterized by canonical 'default-mode networks' (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Mitra and Raichle, 2016; Raichle, 2015) which have been identified in humans (Raichle, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on default-mode networks in humans.

claim: Default-mode networks have been identified in primates.
source: The resting-state of the cortical functional architecture is characterized by canonical 'default-mode networks' (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Mitra and Raichle, 2016; Raichle, 2015) which have been identified in humans (Raichle, 2011), primates (Chauvette et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on default-mode networks in primates.

claim: Default-mode networks have been identified in rodents.
source: The resting-state of the cortical functional architecture is characterized by canonical 'default-mode networks' (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Mitra and Raichle, 2016; Raichle, 2015) which have been identified in humans (Raichle, 2011), primates (Chauvette et al., 2011) and rodents (Gozzi and Schwarz, 2016; Jonckers et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on default-mode networks in rodents.

claim: The spatio-temporal features of resting-state networks are not static.
source: However, the spatio-temporal features of these networks are not static (Deco et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work demonstrating dynamic network features.

claim: Alternating states of excitability can dynamically occur in different brain regions at the same time in the awake condition.
source: Alternating states of excitability, manifesting as different activity states of the brain, can dynamically occur, even in different regions at the same time, as seen in the awake condition (Guo et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on alternating excitability states.

claim: Different states of brain activation can influence responses upon incoming sensory afferents.
source: Different states of brain activation can influence responses upon incoming sensory afferents (Pachitariu et al., 2015; Schwalm et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work showing state-dependent sensory responses.

claim: Different states of brain activation are accompanied by alterations in the spatiotemporal pattern of neuronal activity in many brain areas.
source: Different states of brain activation can influence responses upon incoming sensory afferents (Pachitariu et al., 2015; Schwalm et al., 2017) and are accompanied by alterations in the spatiotemporal pattern of neuronal activity in many brain areas (Pais-Roldán et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on spatiotemporal activity patterns.

claim: Alterations in brain activity states can be observed in local electrophysiological recordings.
source: These alterations can be observed in local electrophysiological (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Deco et al., 2013; Gozzi and Schwarz, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Alterations in brain activity states can be observed in optical recordings.
source: These alterations can be observed in local electrophysiological (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Deco et al., 2013; Gozzi and Schwarz, 2016) and optical (Jonckers et al., 2011; Matsui et al., 2016) recordings
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior optical recording studies.

claim: Alterations in brain activity states can be observed in large-scale BOLD fMRI readouts.
source: These alterations can be observed in local electrophysiological (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011; Deco et al., 2013; Gozzi and Schwarz, 2016) and optical (Jonckers et al., 2011; Matsui et al., 2016) recordings, as well as in large-scale readouts of brain activity, such as BOLD fMRI (Kalthoff et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2009; Staresina et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Two activity states have been identified that occur under different types of anesthesia used for small animal fMRI studies.
source: Recently, using local and brain-wide readouts, we have identified two activity states which were shown to occur under different types of anesthesia used for small animal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies (Schwalm et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work identifying these activity states.

claim: In a state of persistent activity, neurons are rather depolarized and sparsely active, leading to temporally dynamic, modality specific, network configurations.
source: In a state of persistent activity, which can occur during periods of light anesthesia, sedation or during awake periods (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011), neurons are rather depolarized, sparsely active, leading to temporally dynamic, modality specific, network configurations (Barth and Poulet, 2012; D'Souza et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work characterizing persistent activity.

claim: Persistent activity can occur during periods of light anesthesia, sedation or during awake periods.
source: In a state of persistent activity, which can occur during periods of light anesthesia, sedation or during awake periods (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on persistent activity conditions.

claim: Slow oscillations or slow waves have been extensively described under various conditions.
source: In contrast to persistent activity, stands the bimodal activity pattern of slow oscillations, or slow waves which have been extensively described under various conditions (Chauvette et al., 2011; Ma and Zhang, 2018; Petersen et al., 2003; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Schwalm et al., 2017; Seamari et al., 2007; Stroh et al., 2013; Zucca et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on slow waves.

claim: Slow waves have only most recently been studied in the framework of BOLD fMRI.
source: In contrast to persistent activity, stands the bimodal activity pattern of slow oscillations, or slow waves which have been extensively described under various conditions (Chauvette et al., 2011; Ma and Zhang, 2018; Petersen et al., 2003; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Schwalm et al., 2017; Seamari et al., 2007; Stroh et al., 2013; Zucca et al., 2017), but only most recently in the framework of BOLD fMRI (Chang et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2011; Mitra et al., 2015; Schwalm et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent fMRI studies of slow waves.

claim: The low-frequency component of slow waves ranges at 0.2–1 Hz.
source: Their corresponding low-frequency component ranges at 0.2–1 Hz, reflecting alternating activity patterns
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about slow wave frequency characteristics.

claim: Slow waves reflect alternating activity patterns: active ('up') periods in which cells are depolarized and fire action potentials, and silence ('down') periods with hyperpolarized membrane potentials and an almost complete absence of neuronal activity.
source: Their corresponding low-frequency component ranges at 0.2–1 Hz, reflecting alternating activity patterns: active ('up') periods in which cells are depolarized and fire action potentials in temporally restricted periods, and silence ('down') periods with rather hyperpolarized membrane potentials and an almost complete absence of neuronal activity (Destexhe et al., 2007; Steriade et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work characterizing slow wave activity patterns.

claim: Slow waves can occur rather locally.
source: Slow waves can occur rather locally (Nir et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on local slow waves.

claim: Slow waves can spread over the entire cortex.
source: Slow waves can occur rather locally (Nir et al., 2011) or can spread over the entire cortex (Ma and Zhang, 2018; Schwalm et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cortex-wide slow waves.

claim: Slow waves can allow activity to propagate.
source: Slow waves can occur rather locally (Nir et al., 2011) or can spread over the entire cortex (Ma and Zhang, 2018; Schwalm et al., 2017), eventually allowing activity to propagate (Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on slow wave propagation.

claim: Independent component analysis for data obtained during persistent activity revealed canonical resting-state associated networks, such as the default mode.
source: In our previous work, we found that independent component analysis (ICA) for data obtained during persistent activity revealed canonical resting-state associated networks, such as the default mode (Lu et al., 2012; Schwalm et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work including the authors' own previous study.

claim: Independent component analysis for data obtained during persistent activity revealed different sensory networks.
source: In our previous work, we found that independent component analysis (ICA) for data obtained during persistent activity revealed canonical resting-state associated networks, such as the default mode (Lu et al., 2012; Schwalm et al., 2017) or different sensory networks (Liang et al., 2013; Pawela et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on sensory networks.

claim: The bimodality of slow waves is resembled in a plethora of different conditions.
source: However, defining features of slow wave activity, such as its bimodality, are resembled in a plethora of different conditions (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Ma and Zhang, 2018; Mitra et al., 2018; Stroh et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on slow wave bimodality across conditions.

claim: The fundamental difference between fast and slow timescale cortical dynamics is regulated by distinct mechanisms at the single neuron level.
source: likely because the fundamental difference between fast and slow timescale cortical dynamics is regulated by distinct mechanisms at the single neuron level (Okun et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on neuronal mechanisms.

claim: Functional connectivity analysis for resting-state fMRI is used to identify and characterize neural networks in health and disease.
source: Functional connectivity analysis for resting-state fMRI is used to identify and characterize neural networks in health and disease (Buckner et al., 2005; Woodward et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on functional connectivity applications.

claim: Functional connectivity analysis for resting-state fMRI is used during learning.
source: Functional connectivity analysis for resting-state fMRI is used to identify and characterize neural networks in health and disease (Buckner et al., 2005; Woodward et al., 2011), during learning (Lewis et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on learning-related connectivity.

claim: Functional connectivity analysis for resting-state fMRI is used during memory consolidation.
source: Functional connectivity analysis for resting-state fMRI is used to identify and characterize neural networks in health and disease (Buckner et al., 2005; Woodward et al., 2011), during learning (Lewis et al., 2009) or memory consolidation (Staresina et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on memory consolidation connectivity.

claim: Subtle changes in anesthesia level can dramatically change brain connectivity.
source: Despite evidence of subtle changes in anesthesia level being able to dramatically change brain connectivity (Grandjean et al., 2014; Hutchison et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on anesthesia effects on connectivity.

claim: Little has been investigated on how the brain's current state impacts functional connectivity derived from BOLD activity.
source: Despite evidence of subtle changes in anesthesia level being able to dramatically change brain connectivity (Grandjean et al., 2014; Hutchison et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019), little has been investigated on how the brain's current state impacts functional connectivity derived from blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature review indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Variations in functional connectivity have been related to cognitive state in humans.
source: While variations in functional connectivity have been related to cognitive state in humans (Finn et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on cognitive state and connectivity.

claim: The effect of neurophysiologically defined states on functional connectivity in the cortex remains unknown.
source: While variations in functional connectivity have been related to cognitive state in humans (Finn et al., 2017), the effect of neurophysiologically defined states on functional connectivity in the cortex remains unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature review indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: A cortex-wide component was found in all animals during isoflurane-induced slow wave activity.
source: While we found a cortex-wide component in all animals during isoflurane-induced slow wave activity (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The identified components for persistent activity resembled those described by others for awake or sedated rodents.
source: the identified components for persistent activity resembled those described by others for awake (Becerra et al., 2011; Paasonen et al., 2018) or sedated rodents (Bukhari et al., 2018; Schwalm et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited prior work on awake and sedated rodents.

claim: Default mode network activation was identified in 14 of 15 animals during persistent activity.
source: We identified default mode network activation in 14 of 15 animals (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A bilateral auditory component was identified in 11 of 15 medetomidine-sedated animals during persistent activity.
source: a bilateral auditory component in 11 of 15 medetomidine-sedated animals (Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A bilateral component of the insula was identified in 9 of 15 animals during persistent activity.
source: a bilateral component of the insula in 9 of 15 animals (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Four default mode network regions were identified: left and right posterior parietal cortex, anterior and posterior insular cortex and orbital/prelimbic cortex.
source: Similarly, as it has been reported in previous work (Hsu et al., 2016), we identified four default mode network regions: left and right posterior parietal cortex, anterior and posterior insular cortex and orbital/prelimbic cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with cited prior work.

claim: There is a wide distribution of significant connectivity among the different networks during slow wave activity compared with the high specificity showed during persistent activity.
source: When both matrices are compared, it can be observed that there is a wide distribution of significant connectivity among the different networks (delineated by the black squares) during slow wave activity (Figure 1E) compared with the high specificity showed during persistent activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E comparing connectivity matrices.

claim: There are marked differences in the network configurations between slow wave activity and persistent activity.
source: These results indicate that there are marked differences in the network configurations between both types of activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the connectivity matrix comparisons.

claim: The CDF values differed significantly between slow wave activity and persistent activity at the mean of the cutoff (paired t-test, t(14) = 6.01 p<0.001).
source: The CDF values differed significantly between both activity states (paired t-test, t(14) = 6.01 p<0.001) at the mean of the cutoff (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of correlated pairs for each individual at its particular cutoff was significant between slow wave activity and persistent activity (paired t-test, t(14) = 6.502, p<0.001).
source: The number of correlated pairs for each individual at its particular cutoff was significant (paired t-test, t(14) = 6.502, p<0.001) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Slow wave and persistent activity are related to different functional connectivity patterns.
source: These results suggest that slow wave and persistent activity are related to different functional connectivity patterns.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the connectivity analysis results.

claim: During persistent activity, functional connectivity is more compartmentalized than during slow wave activity.
source: from this diagram it is possible to infer that during persistent activity, functional connectivity is more compartmentalized than during slow wave activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the connectivity diagrams shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: During slow wave activity, BOLD-driven connectivity shows a stronger dependency on the distance between areas than during persistent activity (paired t-test, t(14) = 5.43, p<0.001).
source: We found, that this is indeed the case for slow wave activity recordings (Figure 3C), whose slopes are significantly lower than those of data recorded during persistent activity (paired t-test, t(14) = 5.43, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of distance-correlation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: During slow wave activity the BOLD signal is governed by different dynamics than the BOLD signal during persistent activity.
source: These results corroborate that the BOLD signal during slow wave activity is governed by different dynamics than the BOLD signal during persistent activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fALFF and distance-correlation analyses.

claim: During slow wave activity, BOLD-driven connectivity is less compartmentalized than during persistent activity.
source: Furthermore, during slow wave activity, BOLD-driven connectivity seems to be less compartmentalized and shows a stronger dependency on the distance between areas than it is the case for persistent activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the connectivity and distance-correlation analyses.

claim: Modularity values were significantly higher for persistent activity than for slow wave activity (paired t-test, t(14) = 4.01, p=0.001).
source: When we compared modularity values from networks identified for slow wave activity to those of networks identified for persistent activity, we indeed observed significantly higher values for persistent activity (paired t-test, t(14) = 4.01, p=0.001; Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of graph theory metrics shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No significant differences were found in the global efficiency scores between slow wave activity and persistent activity (paired t-test, t(14) = 0.389, p=0.703).
source: When we compared these measures, we did not find significant differences in the global efficiency scores (Figure 4B; paired t-test, t(14) = 0.389, p=0.703)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of graph theory metrics shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Significantly lower scores for slow wave activity than for persistent activity were found in the local efficiency measurement (paired t-test, t(14) = 5.869, p<0.001).
source: but we found significantly lower scores for slow wave activity than for persistent activity in the local efficiency measurement (Figure 4C; paired t-test, t(14) = 5.869, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of graph theory metrics shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A significantly lower clustering coefficient was found for networks dominated by slow wave activity (paired t-test, t(14) = 3.789, p=0.002).
source: In our analyses, we found a significantly lower clustering coefficient for networks dominated by slow wave activity (Figure 4D; paired t-test, t(14) = 3.789, p=0.002)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of graph theory metrics shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant differences were found between networks in slow wave and persistent activity for characteristic path length (paired t-test, t(14) = 0.636, p=0.535).
source: but no significant differences between networks in slow wave and persistent activity for characteristic path length (Figure 4E; paired t-test, t(14) = 0.636, p=0.535).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of graph theory metrics shown in Figure 4E.

claim: During slow wave activity the cortex behaves like a random network, whilst during persistent activity it exhibits small world network features.
source: This suggests that during slow wave activity the cortex rather behaves like a random network, whilst during persistent activity it exhibits small world network features (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the graph theory analysis results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Graph theory analysis indicated a different functional connectivity pattern for persistent and slow wave activity.
source: In summary, graph theory analysis indicated a different functional connectivity pattern for persistent and slow wave activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the graph theory analysis results.

claim: For persistent activity canonical well compartmentalized, small world networks play a dominating role.
source: For persistent activity canonical well compartmentalized, small world networks seem to play a dominating role
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the graph theory analysis results.

claim: During slow wave activity a highly interconnected randomized network is prevalent.
source: while during slow wave activity a highly interconnected randomized network is prevalent.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the graph theory analysis results.

claim: The population dynamics recorded under low isoflurane anesthesia resemble the ones obtained under medetomidine, rather than showing similarity to the ones recorded under higher isoflurane concentrations.
source: In the fiber photometry recordings (Figure 5A), it becomes apparent that the population dynamics recorded under this low isoflurane anesthesia regime resemble the ones obtained under medetomidine, rather than showing similarity to the ones recorded under higher isoflurane concentrations (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The connectivity patterns obtained under the low isoflurane concentration were significantly more similar to those measured under medetomidine (persistent activity) than to those measured under higher isoflurane concentrations (slow wave activity) (paired t-test, t(5) = 5.19, p=0.003).
source: In this case, the resulting values related to persistent activity induced by low isoflurane, were significantly lower when compared with the ones for persistent activity induced by medetomidine sedation than when compared to the ones related to slow wave activity under high isoflurane concentration (Figure 5D; paired t-test, t(5) = 5.19, p=0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of matrix similarity data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the case of persistent activity induced by medetomidine and by low isoflurane concentrations, network configurations were significantly more stable than in the case of slow wave activity induced by high isoflurane concentrations.
source: The results show that in the case of persistent activity induced by medetomidine and by low isoflurane concentrations, network configurations were significantly more stable than in the case of slow wave activity induced by high isoflurane concentrations (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic connectivity analysis data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The network dynamics during slow wave activity might be related to a constant reorganization of connectivity patterns, probably due to the frequent changes in the rate of population down-up transitions.
source: This indicates that the network dynamics during slow wave activity might be related to a constant reorganization of connectivity patterns, probably due to the frequent changes in the rate of population down-up transitions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the dynamic connectivity analysis results.

claim: The CDF data showed significantly higher values for the CWCcov condition at the mean of the cutoff (paired t-test¸ t(14) = 4.96, p<0.001).
source: The CDF data (same analysis as in Figure 2B) showed significantly higher values for the CWCcov condition at the mean of the cutoff (Figure 6Aii) (paired t-test¸ t(14) = 4.96, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of CDF data shown in Figure 6Aii.

claim: The amount of significantly correlated pairs for each individual at its particular cutoff was significantly less in the CWCcov condition (paired t-test, t(14) = 5.435, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, the amount of significantly correlated pairs for each individual at its particular cutoff was also significantly less in the CWCcov condition. (paired t-test, t(14) = 5.435, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of connectivity data with cortex-wide component as covariable.

claim: There is a relationship between slow wave activity-related down-up transitions in the population signal and the strength of cortical functional connectivity.
source: This suggests a relationship between slow wave activity-related down-up transitions in the population signal and the strength of cortical functional connectivity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the covariable analysis results.

claim: The correlation between the amount of down-up transitions in the fluorescence signal and the BOLD pairs was significant for five of the six animals (p<0.001).
source: The correlation between the amount of down-up transitions in the fluorescence signal and the BOLD pairs was significant for five of the six animals (p<0.001) (Figure 6Bii).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data shown in Figure 6Bii.

claim: In the five animals, the permutation test shows that the correlation r-scores are in the 5% of significant values.
source: In the five animals, the permutation test shows that the correlation r-scores are in the 5% of significant values (Figure 6Bii, normal distribution plots).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test results shown in Figure 6Bii.

claim: The repeated measures correlation for the whole dataset was r(196) = 0.534, p<10e−15.
source: Finally, we calculated the statistical value for the whole dataset using the recently described repeated measures correlation (Bakdash and Marusich, 2017) a statistical technique for determining the inter-individuals correlation for intra-subject multiple measurements (r(196) = 0.534, p<10e−15).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using repeated measures correlation.

claim: Slow wave activity-related down-up transitions are directly linked to the increase in cortical functional connectivity during the prevalence of slow waves.
source: These results strongly suggest that slow wave activity-related down-up transitions are directly linked to the increase in cortical functional connectivity during the prevalence of slow waves.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis between down-up transitions and connectivity.

claim: The occurrence of slow waves in a spatially confined neural population can be detected using fiber photometry measuring fluorescent signals emitted by cells previously stained with a calcium indicator.
source: The occurrence of slow waves in a spatially confined neural population can be detected using fiber photometry measuring fluorescent signals emitted by cells previously stained with a calcium indicator (Adelsberger et al., 2014; Grienberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on fiber photometry methods.

claim: Slow wave related down-up transitions have a duration of 2 s on average.
source: Slow wave related down-up transitions can be easily identified and quantified (Seamari et al., 2007) and have a duration of 2 s on average (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and citation to prior work.

claim: The amplitude of the cross-correlation between S1 and V1 signals is significant, with a delay matching the propagation time of the wave propagating from V1 to S1 (51.2 mm/s ± 8.1 s.e.m).
source: The amplitude of the cross-correlation between these two signals is significant (Figure 7D), with a delay matching the propagation time of the wave propagating from V1 to S1 ((n = 6) 51.2 mm/s ± 8.1 s.e.m).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The cross-correlation values were significantly lower when data was filtered between 0.01 and 0.4 Hz (paired t-test: t(5) = 4.26, p=0.008).
source: The cross-correlation values were significantly lower when data was filtered between 0.01 and 0.4 Hz (paired t-test: t(5) = 4.26, p=0.008)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of filtered cross-correlation data.

claim: The cross-correlation values were significantly lower when data was filtered between 0.2–0.6 Hz (paired t-test: t(5) = 7.99, p<0.001).
source: The cross-correlation values were significantly lower when data was filtered between 0.01 and 0.4 Hz (paired t-test: t(5) = 4.26, p=0.008), 0.2–0.6 Hz (t(5) = 7.99, p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of filtered cross-correlation data.

claim: The cross-correlation values were significantly lower when data was filtered between 0.3–0.7 Hz (paired t-test: t(5) = 7.28, p<0.001).
source: The cross-correlation values were significantly lower when data was filtered between 0.01 and 0.4 Hz (paired t-test: t(5) = 4.26, p=0.008), 0.2–0.6 Hz (t(5) = 7.99, p<0.001), and 0.3–0.7 (t(5) = 7.28, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of filtered cross-correlation data.

claim: Down-up transitions are the main contributor to an increase of cortical functional connectivity during slow wave activity.
source: These results support the ones obtained previously with BOLD connectivity analyses at the cortical population level, demonstrating down-up transitions to be the main contributor to an increase of cortical functional connectivity during slow wave activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the filtered cross-correlation analysis results.

claim: Different states of brain activity can modify properties of the functional connectome.
source: We demonstrated that different states of brain activity can modify properties of the functional connectome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overall experimental results.

claim: ICA showed distinct functional networks for each of the investigated activity states.
source: ICA showed distinct functional networks for each of the investigated activity states.
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICA analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the case of slow wave activity, a cortex-wide component was found in all animals.
source: In the case of slow wave activity, a cortex-wide component was found in all animals
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICA analysis results.

claim: For persistent activity, a clear compartmentalization of the cortical functional structures gave origin to well-determined functional networks, as the default mode or the auditory network.
source: while for persistent activity, a clear compartmentalization of the cortical functional structures gave origin to well-determined functional networks, as the default mode or the auditory network.
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICA analysis results.

claim: The relation of population activity to functional connectivity was not dependent on a specific anesthetic agent.
source: Notably, the relation of population activity to functional connectivity was not dependent on a specific anesthetic agent
evidence: This claim is supported by the low isoflurane experiments showing similar results to medetomidine.

claim: Not the type of anesthesia used, but the induced activity state influenced resting-state networks.
source: suggesting that not the type of anesthesia used, but the induced activity state influenced resting-state networks.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of different anesthetic protocols.

claim: Population activity dominated by slow waves is characterized by long periods of quiescence followed by short lapses of neural activity corresponding to a propagating wave.
source: Population activity dominated by slow waves is characterized by long periods of quiescence followed by short lapses of neural activity corresponding to a propagating wave (Stroh et al., 2013), as demonstrated by the simultaneous dual cortical calcium recordings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and the dual cortical calcium recordings in this study.

claim: The high degree of compartmentalization in persistent activity dominated networks observed in the ICA can be corroborated by calculating the dependency of the distance in the r-scores between two areas.
source: The high degree of compartmentalization in persistent activity dominated networks, observed in the ICA can be corroborated by calculating the dependency of the distance in the r-scores between two areas.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the distance-correlation analysis.

claim: In a highly compartmentalized connectome, the dependency on Euclidean distance should be lower than in a system which is highly interconnected.
source: In a highly compartmentalized connectome, this dependency should be lower than in a system which is highly interconnected (Hagmann et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: The functional architecture during persistent activity is dominated by specific compartmentalized network nodes, which are not necessarily spatially close, such as the default mode network.
source: This finding suggests, that indeed, the functional architecture during persistent activity is dominated by specific compartmentalized network nodes, which are not necessarily spatially close, such as the default mode network.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the distance-correlation analysis results.

claim: During slow wave activity, a strong distance dependency was observed, in line with a propagating wave of activity.
source: In sharp contrast, during slow wave activity, we observed a strong distance dependency, in line with a propagating wave of activity – a slow wave event – eventually recruiting large parts of the cortex.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the distance-correlation analysis results.

claim: Propagating slow wave events might temporarily switch parts of the functional network from a hyperpolarized, rather quiescent down state into a depolarized up state of high excitability and thereby propagate over cortical areas.
source: These propagating slow wave events might temporarily switch parts of the functional network from a hyperpolarized, rather quiescent down state into a depolarized up state of high excitability and thereby propagate over cortical areas (Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Steriade et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by citations to prior work on slow wave mechanisms.

claim: During persistent activity the functional network shows characteristic small world network dynamics, as they have been described previously for the sedated rat and for the awake human brain.
source: Applying graph theory methods, we found that during persistent activity the functional network shows characteristic small world network dynamics, as they have been described previously for the sedated rat (D'Souza et al., 2014) and for the awake human brain (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by graph theory analysis results and citations to prior work.

claim: During slow wave activity graph theory analysis demonstrated characteristics of highly interconnected random networks to be dominant.
source: During slow wave activity graph theory analysis demonstrated characteristics of highly interconnected random networks to be dominant, corroborating the idea of a lack of a spatially segregated functional connectivity signature in that state (Okun et al., 2019; Spoormaker et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by graph theory analysis results and citations to prior work.

claim: Decreasing the amount of isoflurane administrated to the animal led to a transition from slow wave to persistent activity.
source: In order to rule out anesthesia-specific effects on connectivity, we demonstrated that decreasing the amount of isoflurane administrated to the animal led to a transition from slow wave to persistent activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the low isoflurane experiments.

claim: Population and functional connectivity dynamics observed under a low dose of isoflurane rather resembled the ones observed under medetomidine-induced persistent activity, than the ones observed during slow wave activity induced by high isoflurane anesthesia.
source: Indeed, population and functional connectivity dynamics observed under a low dose of isoflurane rather resembled the ones observed under medetomidine-induced persistent activity, than the ones observed during slow wave activity induced by high isoflurane anesthesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the low isoflurane experiments.

claim: Spontaneous resting-state associated brain activity is non-random in the temporal domain and this feature is well conserved for rodents and humans.
source: Recently, it is has been shown that spontaneous resting-state associated brain activity is non-random in the temporal domain and that this feature is well conserved for rodents and humans (Ma and Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on temporal dynamics of resting-state activity.

claim: Animals in persistent activity state showed rather temporally stable - persistent - connectivity dynamics.
source: Interestingly, when we analyzed the temporal dynamics of connectivity patterns, we found that animals in persistent activity state, induced either by medetomidine or a low dose of isoflurane, showed rather temporally stable - persistent - connectivity dynamics (Destexhe et al., 2007; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Steriade et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic connectivity analysis results and citations to prior work.

claim: Animals in slow wave activity state showed fast, and temporally irregular transitions likely reflecting the bimodality of slow waves.
source: In contrast, animals in slow wave activity state showed fast, and temporally irregular transitions likely reflecting the bimodality of slow waves (Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic connectivity analysis results and citation to prior work.

claim: Individual specific events within slow wave activity could drive state-specific network signatures.
source: This suggests that individual specific events within slow wave activity could drive state-specific network signatures
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the dynamic connectivity analysis results.

claim: The regularity of down-up transitions or slow wave events can depend on the overall physiological condition of the animal, such as the depth of anesthesia.
source: while it has to be taken into account that the regularity of down-up transitions or slow wave events can depend on the overall physiological condition of the animal, such as the depth of anesthesia (Chauvette et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on factors affecting slow wave regularity.

claim: There is abundant evidence on the relevance of infra-slow electrical brain activity for resting state connectivity.
source: Although, there is abundant evidence on the relevance of, for example, infra-slow electrical brain activity for resting state connectivity (Hiltunen et al., 2014; Krishnan et al., 2018; Mitra et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on infra-slow activity.

claim: There has been no evidence linking different population activity states of the brain to changes in functional network configuration directly.
source: there so far has been no evidence linking different population activity states of the brain to changes in functional network configuration directly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature review indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: When the cortex-wide component was used as a covariable in the connectivity analyses, the connectivity values decreased significantly.
source: When we used the cortex-wide component as a covariable in the connectivity analyses, the connectivity values decreased significantly.
evidence: This claim is supported by the covariable analysis results.

claim: The cortex-wide component represents a direct correlate of slow wave activity in a local neural population.
source: This component represents a direct correlate of slow wave activity in a local neural population (Schwalm et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The generation and propagation of slow waves is depending on changes in cortical excitability during sleep or under anesthesia.
source: It has been suggested that the generation and propagation of slow waves is depending on changes in cortical excitability during sleep (Massimini et al., 2004) or under anesthesia (Ruiz-Mejias et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on slow wave generation.

claim: Slow wave propagation can differentially affect cortical layers.
source: even differentially affecting cortical layers (Capone et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on layer-specific effects.

claim: Disrupted slow wave propagation can be reflective of pathophysiological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: Disrupted slow wave propagation can be reflective of pathophysiological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease (Busche et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on pathological slow waves.

claim: Distinct activity states of the brain, that is defined spatio-temporal dynamics of cortical excitability, drive the brain's functional connectivity.
source: We therefore propose that distinct activity states of the brain, that is defined spatio-temporal dynamics of cortical excitability, drive the brain's functional connectivity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overall experimental results.

claim: The understanding of network dynamics underlying respective functional network patterns will reduce the variability found in resting-state data and increase the translational value of resting-state fMRI studies performed in rodents.
source: The understanding of network dynamics underlying respective functional network patterns will reduce the variability found in resting-state data and increase the translational value of resting-state fMRI studies performed in rodents.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: The functional state of the brain is dynamic over time, and this is reflected in changes in functional connectivity.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that the functional state of the brain is dynamic over time, and that this is reflected in changes in functional connectivity (Belloy et al., 2018; Grandjean et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on dynamic functional connectivity.

claim: Dynamic states are quantifiable, depend on ongoing activity and seem to show atypical dynamics in some neurological disorders.
source: These dynamic states are quantifiable, depend on ongoing activity and seem to show atypical dynamics in some neurological disorders (Gutierrez-Barragan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on dynamic states in disorders.

claim: Degrees of wakefulness play an important role in global functional connectivity.
source: Degrees of wakefulness seem to play an important role in global functional connectivity (Turchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on wakefulness and connectivity.

claim: During resting-state recordings in humans, dynamic changes in functional connectivity occur depending on different wakefulness and sleep patterns.
source: One study showed that during resting-state recordings in humans, dynamic changes in functional connectivity occur depending on different wakefulness and sleep patterns (Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on sleep-related connectivity changes.

claim: The dynamic variability over time in fMRI functional connectivity signatures can be explained by fluctuating sleep stages.
source: More recently, Laumann and colleagues showed that the dynamic variability over time in fMRI functional connectivity signatures can be explained by fluctuating sleep stages (Laumann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on sleep stage effects.

claim: Anesthetized animals show lower functional coupling than awake animals.
source: Previous resting-state fMRI studies report that anesthetized animals show lower functional coupling than awake animals (Vincent et al., 2007; Yin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on anesthesia effects.

claim: Default mode networks in rodents can be found even after the loss of consciousness.
source: However, some studies show that default mode networks in rodents can be found even after the loss of consciousness (Liang et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on default mode networks under anesthesia.

claim: Some studies show a breakdown in the networks of resting state connectivity under anesthesia.
source: while others show a breakdown in the networks of resting state connectivity under anesthesia (Boveroux et al., 2010; Stamatakis et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on connectivity breakdown under anesthesia.

claim: Dissimilar results on connectivity under anesthesia have been hypothesized to be dependent on the synchronization of infra-slow oscillatory activity and cross-frequency coupling.
source: These apparent dissimilar results have been hypothesized to be dependent on the synchronization of infra-slow oscillatory activity and cross-frequency coupling (Hutchison et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work proposing this hypothesis.

claim: The origin of discrepancies in connectivity results may lie in the presence of different activity states of the brain.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that the origin of these discrepancies may lie in the presence of different activity states of the brain.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: During persistent activity, compartmentalized patterns are detected, whilst during slow wave activity the degree of connectivity depends on the rate of slow waves generated in a particular period of time.
source: During persistent activity, compartmentalized patterns are detected, whilst during slow wave activity the degree of connectivity depends on the rate of slow waves generated in a particular period of time.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Global signal removal has been shown to reduce connectivity for high isoflurane global synchrony conditions.
source: Global signal removal has been shown to reduce connectivity for high isoflurane global synchrony conditions (Grandjean et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on global signal removal.

claim: Global signal removal might be removing the underlying down-up transition related signals which are actually explaining a relevant part of the increased connectivity.
source: This might indeed be because this technique is removing the underlying down-up transition related signals which are actually explaining a relevant part of the increased connectivity as our results show.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the covariable analysis results.

claim: Activity states of the brain as well as the rate of down-up transitions during slow wave activity in particular are dynamic and can be present under different experimental settings.
source: Activity states of the brain as well as the rate of down-up transitions during slow wave activity in particular are dynamic and can be present under different experimental settings (Vyazovskiy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on dynamic activity states.

claim: In awake animals or during slow wave sleep, the entire cortex might not be engaged in either persistent or slow wave activity.
source: Here, we present data from strictly controlled conditions, in which the entire cortex seems to be engaged in either persistent or slow wave activity. However, in awake animals or during slow wave sleep, this might not be the case.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about conditions beyond the experimental setup.

claim: Human subjects may transition between similar subtypes of activity states when they transition between different levels of attention during an experiment or when they fall asleep.
source: Human subjects may transition between similar subtypes of these activity states when they transition between different levels of attention during an experiment or when they fall asleep (Stevner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Animals may react differently to the same anaesthetic regimen and therefore present a different underlying state of cortical activity while being subjected to the same anaesthesia condition.
source: Even more so, animals may react differently to the same anaesthetic regimen (Vyazovskiy et al., 2011) and therefore present a different underlying state of cortical activity while being subjected to the same anaesthesia condition.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An animal may be in a state of persistent activity at the beginning of an imaging experiment, and shift into a state of slow wave activity due to a change of underlying physiology or deepened anaesthesia over time.
source: Similarly, it might be the case that at the beginning of an imaging experiment, an animal is in a state of persistent activity, and while the experiment progresses, shifts into a state of slow wave activity due to a change of underlying physiology or deepened anaesthesia over time.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about potential experimental scenarios.

claim: It is necessary to consider the particular activity state and global changes in cortical excitability before deriving conclusions about networks dynamics in any resting-state fMRI experiment.
source: As our results show that this would lead to drastically different functional connectivity signatures, it is necessary to consider the particular activity state and global changes in cortical excitability before deriving conclusions about networks dynamics in any resting-state fMRI experiment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overall experimental results and their implications.

claim: Experiments were performed on 25 adult female Lewis rats (>12 weeks old, 160–200 g).
source: Experiments were performed on 25 adult female Lewis rats (>12 weeks old, 160–200 g)
evidence: This claim is a direct statement of the experimental methods.

claim: 15 animals were used for fMRI measurements.
source: of which 15 were used for fMRI measurements
evidence: This claim is a direct statement of the experimental methods.

claim: Six animals were implanted with an optic fiber in the visual cortex for combined optic-fiber-based calcium recordings/fMRI measurements.
source: six were implanted with an optic fiber in the visual cortex for combined optic-fiber-based calcium recordings/fMRI measurements
evidence: This claim is a direct statement of the experimental methods.

claim: Four animals were used for optical recordings on the bench.
source: and four were used for optical recordings on the bench.
evidence: This claim is a direct statement of the experimental methods.
